title: Health & protection insurance
recap: PMI pays for private treatment of acute conditions that start after joining; chronic care, emergencies, routine maternity, cosmetic work and most GP care are out.
Moratorium excludes the last five years' conditions with no forms (they can lift after two clear years); full medical underwriting names exclusions up front; groups can get MHD or CPME.

Protection pays money: income protection (monthly, after a deferred period, part of salary, own occupation is best), critical illness (lump sum after a survival period) and life cover (term or whole-of-life).
Health brokers run a yearly cycle for employers: design and place cover, support and advocate on claims, fight the renewal using claims data, and add wellbeing extras like EAPs and virtual GPs.
PMI complements the NHS, usually starting with a GP referral, and waiting lists drive demand; your clinical grasp of pathways and conditions is a real edge.

sections.heading: PMI: what it is and what it pays for
sections.body:
Private medical insurance (PMI) pays for private diagnosis and treatment of conditions that start after you join. You'll also hear it called health insurance or private health cover. It comes in two main forms.

- **Individual PMI** is bought by a person for themselves or their family, and they pay the premium (the price of the policy).
- **Group or corporate PMI** is bought by an employer for its staff, usually as a perk alongside salary.

Group cover is the bigger part of a health broker's world, so it's where most of your conversations will sit.

### Acute vs chronic: the idea everything hangs on

PMI is built for **acute** conditions. An acute condition is an illness or injury that's likely to respond quickly to treatment and get you back to how you were before: a hernia repair, a cataract, a torn knee ligament, investigating a worrying lump.

A **chronic** condition goes on indefinitely. It has no known cure, needs ongoing monitoring or management, or tends to come back. Diabetes, asthma, Crohn's disease and multiple sclerosis are classic examples. You'll recognise the split straight away: it's roughly the line between an episode of care and long-term condition management.

Most policies will pay to find out what's wrong, and many will cover an acute flare-up of a chronic condition. What they won't usually fund is the long-term management: routine reviews, repeat prescriptions and ongoing care. That stays with the NHS.

### What's usually in, and what's usually out

Typically covered, within the policy's limits:

- specialist consultations and diagnostic tests, such as scans and blood tests
- in-patient and day-patient treatment, including surgery
- cancer treatment, a major part of most policies and one that varies a lot between them
- some out-patient therapies, such as physiotherapy, and often mental health treatment

Typically excluded:

- **pre-existing conditions**: anything you had symptoms of, or treatment or advice for, before joining (how this works depends on underwriting, coming next)
- **chronic conditions**, as above
- **emergencies and A&E**: if you have a heart attack or break your leg, the NHS looks after you
- **routine maternity**: normal pregnancy and childbirth, although some policies cover certain complications
- **cosmetic treatment** that isn't medically needed
- **GP services** in general, although many policies now include a virtual GP

Policies are then shaped by options that change the price, such as an excess (the amount the member pays towards a claim), a hospital list that limits where treatment can happen, and caps on out-patient spending.

sections.heading: Underwriting, cash plans and dental
sections.body:
Underwriting is how an insurer decides what it will cover for you. In PMI that mostly means how it treats your medical history. Brokers explain the main options constantly.

### Moratorium underwriting

With **moratorium** underwriting, there's no medical questionnaire. Instead, the policy automatically excludes any condition you've had symptoms, treatment, medication or advice for in the five years before joining.

The clever part is that this exclusion can lift. If you then go two continuous years on the policy with no symptoms, treatment, medication or advice for that condition, it can become eligible. Buying is quick, but there's uncertainty: nobody knows for sure what's covered until a claim comes in and the insurer checks your history.

### Full medical underwriting

With **full medical underwriting** (FMU), you give your medical history up front. The insurer reviews it and names any exclusions in your policy documents. It takes longer to set up but gives certainty: you know from day one what's excluded, and claims tend to run more smoothly because the checking is already done. It also links back to the duty to answer questions honestly from earlier modules.

### Group options

Employers get extra choices, and explaining them is one of the places a broker adds real value:

- **Medical history disregarded (MHD)**: the insurer ignores members' past medical history, so pre-existing conditions can be covered. It's the most generous basis, costs more, and is usually only offered to larger groups.
- **Continued personal medical exclusions (CPME)**: used when an employer moves its scheme to a new insurer. Each member keeps the exclusions they already had, and nobody picks up new ones just because the scheme switched.

Smaller group schemes are often written on moratorium or FMU terms instead.

### Cash plans and dental

A **health cash plan** is a simpler, lower-cost product. It pays fixed amounts back towards everyday healthcare costs, such as dental check-ups, glasses, physiotherapy and prescriptions, up to an annual limit for each category. Many employers offer one to all staff, sometimes alongside PMI for senior roles.

**Dental insurance** focuses on teeth: check-ups, hygienist visits, fillings and other treatment, and often emergency dental care, again within limits. Depending on the plan, it can be used with NHS or private dentists.

sections.heading: Protection: income, illness and life
sections.body:
Protection insurance pays money rather than paying for treatment. These are mostly **benefit** policies, the idea from the indemnity module: they pay an agreed amount when a defined event happens, rather than restoring an exact financial loss.

### Income protection

**Income protection** (IP) pays a regular monthly income if you can't work because of illness or injury. Most people have never heard of it, yet it covers one of the risks most likely to hit a working adult: months off sick.

Three features shape every IP policy:

- **The deferred period.** This is the wait between stopping work and the first payment, anything from a few weeks to a year. A longer deferred period makes cover cheaper, and people often match it to when their sick pay runs out.
- **The benefit.** IP pays a proportion of your earnings, not all of them, often somewhere around half to two-thirds. Leaving a gap keeps an incentive to return to work and stops anyone being better off ill than working.
- **The definition of incapacity.** This is the test of whether you count as unable to work. **Own occupation** means you can't do your own job, so a surgeon with a hand injury can claim even if she could still teach. Stricter tests, such as suited or any occupation, ask whether you could do some other work instead.

Payments usually continue until you go back to work, the benefit period ends, or you reach the policy's end age.

### Critical illness

**Critical illness** (CI) cover pays a one-off lump sum when you're diagnosed with a condition listed in the policy, such as many cancers, a heart attack or a stroke. Each condition has a precise definition, often with a severity threshold, and the diagnosis has to meet it.

Most policies also have a **survival period**: you must survive a set time after diagnosis, often around 10 to 14 days, before the money is paid. The money can be spent on anything.

### Life cover

**Life insurance** pays a lump sum when the insured person dies. **Term** cover runs for a fixed period, say 25 years, and pays only if death happens within it; it's often used to protect a mortgage or a young family, and the sum can stay level or decrease alongside a repayment mortgage. **Whole-of-life** cover lasts as long as premiums are paid and pays out whenever death happens, so it costs more and is often used for estate planning.

sections.heading: Group risk and how health broking works
sections.body:
### Group risk

**Group risk** is the employer version of protection. Rather than each person buying their own policy, the employer buys one policy covering everyone in the scheme.

- **Group life**, often called **death in service**, pays a lump sum, usually a multiple of salary, if an employee dies while employed. It's normally paid through a trust, so the money can reach the family quickly.
- **Group income protection** pays a proportion of salary to staff on long-term sick leave after a deferred period, often set to start when company sick pay ends. The benefit usually goes to the employer, which passes it on through payroll. Good schemes add early intervention and rehabilitation to help people back to work.
- **Group critical illness** pays a lump sum to an employee diagnosed with a listed condition.

One line worth knowing: the **free cover limit** is the level of benefit up to which members are covered automatically, without giving individual medical evidence.

### What a health broker actually does

In this field, brokers often call themselves **employee benefits consultants**. The client is usually an employer, and the job is to help it design, buy and run a benefits package that suits its people and its budget. The work follows a yearly cycle:

1. **Understand the client.** Who are the staff, what's the budget, and what problem is the employer solving: recruitment, retention, sickness absence, morale?
2. **Design and place the cover.** Compare insurers, recommend a scheme design, and negotiate terms.
3. **Support members through the year.** Help with claims that stall or are declined, explain what the policy says, and push back when the insurer seems to have got it wrong. This is **advocacy**: you're on the client's side.
4. **Manage the renewal.** Before each anniversary the insurer reviews the scheme's **claims data** (what's been claimed, and for what) and proposes new rates. Medical costs tend to rise faster than general prices, and a heavy claims year can mean a sharp increase. The broker analyses the claims, challenges the insurer's assumptions, tests the market and suggests design changes, such as an excess or a different hospital list, to keep the scheme affordable.

Claims data is health information, which UK GDPR treats as **special category data** needing extra protection, so employers usually see it anonymised and grouped rather than by named person.

### Wellbeing and add-ons

Schemes now do far more than pay claims. Common extras include:

- an **employee assistance programme** (EAP): a confidential helpline offering short-term counselling and practical advice on money, legal and family worries
- a **virtual GP**: phone or video appointments, often available quickly
- **mental health pathways**: fast, structured routes into talking therapies or specialist support, sometimes without a GP referral
- physiotherapy pathways, health checks and wellbeing apps

A good broker helps the client get people using these, not just paying for them.

sections.heading: The NHS, private care and where you fit
sections.body:
### How PMI and the NHS fit together

PMI complements the NHS rather than replacing it. Someone with PMI is still an NHS patient for emergencies, GP care, maternity and long-term conditions, and can choose either route for planned treatment.

The usual gateway is a **GP referral**. The member sees a GP (NHS, or a virtual GP provided by the insurer), is referred to a specialist, then contacts the insurer to confirm cover before booking. That check is called **pre-authorisation**. Many insurers now suggest a shortlist of consultants, and some let members refer themselves for things like physiotherapy or mental health support.

Many consultants work in both systems, holding an NHS post and running a private practice alongside it. What PMI mainly buys is speed, choice of timing and hospital, and comfort, such as a private room.

The biggest driver of demand is **NHS waiting-list pressure**. When waits for scans and planned surgery grow, employers see staff off sick or struggling at work while they wait, and individuals look for a faster route. That's why PMI is often sold to employers on absence and productivity as much as on perk value.

### Why your clinical background is an advantage

Most people in health broking pick up the clinical side on the job. You'd arrive with it. In practice that means you can:

- **understand pathways**: you know how referral, diagnosis and treatment actually flow, so you can see where a scheme design will help people or leave them stuck
- **read conditions properly**: acute versus chronic isn't abstract to you, which makes cover questions and claim disputes much easier to unpick
- **see the person behind a claim**: a claims report is a table of numbers, but you know what a cancer pathway or a long mental health absence means for someone and their family
- **talk to clinicians and HR as an equal**: you can follow an insurer's clinical team and then explain it plainly to an HR director
- **judge what's clinically sensible**: for example, whether a musculoskeletal pathway, a weight-management or dietetic service, or a mental health offer will genuinely help this particular workforce

You won't give clinical advice in a broking role, and you'll still need the insurance and regulation from the earlier modules. But that combination is rare, and clients notice it.

whyItMatters: This is the day job of a health broking team: explaining what a scheme will and won't pay for, getting renewals right, and standing beside members when a claim goes wrong. Talking fluently about acute versus chronic, underwriting bases and group risk is what will make you credible in that first conversation.

questions.stem: In private medical insurance, what does an 'acute' condition mean?
options: An illness or injury likely to respond quickly to treatment and return you to your previous state of health
Any condition that is severe or life-threatening when it's diagnosed
A condition that has needed hospital treatment at least once in the last five years
A long-term condition that is currently well controlled with medication
questions.explanation: Acute is about whether treatment can get you back to how you were, not about how serious the condition is. PMI is built around that kind of fixable, time-limited episode of care.

questions.stem: Poppy's friend Sam has had type 1 diabetes since childhood and has just joined an employer whose PMI scheme covers pre-existing conditions. Sam hopes the policy will pay for routine diabetes clinic reviews and insulin. What's the most likely answer?
options: Yes, because the scheme covers pre-existing conditions
Only once Sam has been on the scheme for two years without symptoms
No, because ongoing management of a chronic condition is generally excluded and stays with the NHS
Only if Sam pays an excess at each clinic visit
questions.explanation: Covering pre-existing conditions doesn't remove the chronic exclusion: PMI is designed for acute care, so routine long-term diabetes management stays with the NHS. Some policies may help with an acute flare-up, but not the ongoing care.

questions.stem: Which statement about what PMI typically covers is true?
options: Routine pregnancy and childbirth are normally covered as standard
A&E visits are covered so members can skip NHS emergency waits
Cosmetic surgery is covered as long as the member pays the excess
Diagnostic tests, such as scans to investigate new symptoms, are usually covered
questions.explanation: Finding out what's wrong is core PMI territory. Routine maternity, emergencies and A&E, and cosmetic treatment that isn't medically needed are all standard exclusions.

questions.stem: Poppy's colleague breaks her ankle at netball and is taken to A&E, where it's treated. Weeks later her consultant recommends planned surgery to repair the ligaments. She has PMI with no relevant exclusions. How is PMI most likely to respond?
options: It pays for the A&E visit but not the later surgery
It doesn't pay for the A&E care, but the planned surgery may be covered privately
It pays for nothing, because the injury started as an emergency
It pays for both, because every injury counts as acute
questions.explanation: Emergency care sits with the NHS, so A&E isn't covered. Once things are stable, planned treatment of an acute problem is exactly what PMI is for, subject to referral and pre-authorisation.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between individual and group PMI?
options: Group PMI is bought by an employer to cover its staff, while individual PMI is bought by a person for themselves or their family
Group PMI covers emergency care, while individual PMI does not
Individual PMI must be fully medically underwritten, while group PMI never involves underwriting
Group PMI pays a fixed cash amount per treatment, while individual PMI pays the hospital directly
questions.explanation: The difference is who buys it and who's covered. Both are built around acute treatment, and both can be set up on different underwriting bases.

questions.stem: Under moratorium underwriting, which conditions are excluded when the policy starts?
options: Only conditions the member lists on a medical questionnaire
Every condition the member has had at any point in their life
Conditions the member had symptoms, treatment, medication or advice for in roughly the five years before joining
Only conditions a GP has formally diagnosed in the last two years
questions.explanation: Moratorium needs no questionnaire: it automatically excludes recent conditions using a look-back period, typically five years. Listing conditions on a questionnaire is how full medical underwriting works.

questions.stem: Poppy's brother joined an individual PMI policy on moratorium terms eight months ago. He saw a physio for knee pain three years before joining. Now the knee has flared up and he wants a private MRI. What's the most likely outcome?
options: It's covered, because the physio visit was more than two years before he joined
It's covered, because he didn't declare anything and so has no exclusions
It's covered, as long as he gets a GP referral first
It's likely to be excluded for now, because he had treatment for the knee within five years before joining
questions.explanation: The five-year look-back catches the physio treatment, so the knee is excluded. It could become eligible later, but only after two continuous years on the policy free of symptoms, treatment and advice for it.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of full medical underwriting compared with moratorium?
options: There's no need to share any medical history
The member knows from the start exactly which conditions are excluded
Pre-existing conditions are always covered
Exclusions automatically fall away after two symptom-free years
questions.explanation: With full medical underwriting the insurer reviews your history up front and names exclusions on the policy, so there's certainty from day one. Exclusions that can lift after a clear spell are a feature of moratorium.

questions.stem: An employer's PMI scheme is written on a 'medical history disregarded' basis. What does that mean for its staff?
options: Their chronic conditions will be managed long-term by the insurer
Their medical history is hidden from the employer but used to set personal exclusions
Their pre-existing conditions can be covered, because the insurer ignores past medical history
They must each complete a full medical questionnaire before joining
questions.explanation: MHD is the most generous group basis: past medical history is set aside, so pre-existing conditions are eligible. It doesn't turn PMI into chronic-care cover, and it's usually reserved for larger groups.

questions.stem: An employer moves its PMI scheme to a new insurer on 'continued personal medical exclusions' terms. What happens to members?
options: They keep the exclusions they had under the old scheme, with no new ones added because of the switch
All their exclusions are wiped, giving everyone a clean start
They must all be fully medically underwritten again
The new insurer applies a fresh five-year moratorium to everyone
questions.explanation: CPME carries existing personal exclusions across so nobody is worse off for switching. Wiping exclusions altogether would be medical history disregarded, a different and more generous basis.

questions.stem: Which statement about health cash plans is true?
options: They pay for major surgery in a private hospital with no upper limit
They pay a lump sum on diagnosis of a listed serious illness
They can only be bought by individuals and are never offered through employers
They pay fixed amounts back towards everyday costs such as dental check-ups, glasses and physio, up to annual limits
questions.explanation: A cash plan is a low-cost way to help with routine healthcare bills, with a limit per category each year, and employers commonly offer them. Lump sums on diagnosis describe critical illness cover.

questions.stem: Which of these is most typical of a dental insurance plan?
options: Unlimited cosmetic dentistry such as whitening and veneers
Contributions towards check-ups, hygienist visits and treatment, often with emergency dental cover, within set limits
Cover only for dental work needed after an accident at work
Cover included automatically in every PMI policy at no extra cost
questions.explanation: Dental plans focus on routine and restorative care plus emergencies, within annual limits. Cosmetic work is usually excluded, and dental isn't standard in PMI, so it's often bought separately or as an add-on.

questions.stem: In income protection, what is the deferred period?
options: The time a policy must have been held before any claim is allowed
The time between stopping work through illness or injury and the first benefit payment
The maximum length of time benefit will be paid on a claim
The period after a claim during which premiums are paused
questions.explanation: The deferred period is the wait at the start of a claim, and choosing a longer one makes cover cheaper. The maximum time benefit is paid is a separate feature, the benefit period.

questions.stem: A dental surgeon with an own-occupation income protection policy develops a tremor that stops her doing clinical work. She could still teach dental students. What happens?
options: She can't claim, because she is still able to do some kind of work
She receives a lump sum instead of a monthly income
She can claim only if a tremor is on the policy's list of named conditions
She can claim, because she can't do her own job, even though she could do other work
questions.explanation: Own occupation asks whether you can do your own job, which makes it the most generous definition. Under a stricter suited- or any-occupation test, her ability to teach might stop the claim.

questions.stem: Which statement about income protection is true?
options: It usually pays a proportion of earnings rather than full salary, which keeps an incentive to return to work
It pays a single lump sum once the deferred period ends
It replaces all of the member's salary so they are no worse off
It only pays if the illness is on a list of specified critical conditions
questions.explanation: IP pays a regular income capped at a proportion of earnings, so nobody is better off ill than working. A lump sum for a listed condition describes critical illness cover.

questions.stem: In a typical UK group income protection scheme, who usually receives the benefit payments from the insurer?
options: The employee's GP, who manages the return-to-work plan
The employee directly, as a single lump sum
The employer, which passes the money on to the employee through payroll
The NHS, to fund the employee's treatment
questions.explanation: Group IP benefit normally goes to the employer, which keeps the person on payroll and pays them that way. Group critical illness is different: it pays a lump sum to the employee.

questions.stem: What is the survival period in a critical illness policy?
options: A set time, often around 10 to 14 days, that the person must survive after diagnosis before the lump sum is paid
The number of years the person must live after buying the policy before they can claim
The length of time over which the lump sum is paid in instalments
The period after a claim during which any life cover is suspended
questions.explanation: CI pays on diagnosis of a listed condition, but most policies require you to survive a short period first. It's a brief wait after diagnosis, not a waiting period after buying the cover.

questions.stem: Poppy's uncle has critical illness cover and a separate life policy. He has a major heart attack that meets the CI definition but sadly dies five days later. The CI policy has a 14-day survival period. What's most likely?
options: Both policies pay out in full
Neither policy pays, because the death followed a listed condition
The critical illness policy pays, because the diagnosis met the definition
The critical illness policy doesn't pay because the survival period wasn't met, but the life policy pays out
questions.explanation: Meeting the condition definition isn't enough if the survival period isn't met. Life cover pays on death, so his family still receives that lump sum.

questions.stem: How does whole-of-life cover differ from term cover?
options: It pays out if the person is still alive when the policy ends
It pays out whenever death happens, as long as premiums are paid, rather than only within a fixed period
It covers only deaths caused by accidents
It costs less than term cover because it runs for longer
questions.explanation: Whole-of-life has no end date, so a payout is certain if premiums are kept up, which is why it costs more than term cover. Term cover pays only if death happens within the chosen period.

questions.stem: Poppy and her partner buy a flat with a 25-year repayment mortgage. They want life cover that would clear the remaining debt if one of them died, at the lowest sensible cost. Which fits best?
options: Whole-of-life cover for a fixed sum
Income protection with a 13-week deferred period
Decreasing term cover, where the sum insured reduces roughly in line with the mortgage
Critical illness cover with a 14-day survival period
questions.explanation: A repayment mortgage shrinks over time, so cover that shrinks alongside it does the job for less. Whole-of-life would work but costs far more for a debt that ends after 25 years.

questions.stem: What does group life cover, often called death in service, provide?
options: A pension for employees who retire early because of ill health
A lump sum, usually a multiple of salary, if an employee dies while employed
Private treatment for employees with life-threatening conditions
A monthly income for staff on long-term sick leave
questions.explanation: Death in service pays a lump sum, typically a multiple of salary, normally through a trust so the family can be paid quickly. A monthly income during long-term sickness is group income protection.

questions.stem: In group risk schemes, what is the free cover limit?
options: The level of benefit up to which members are covered without giving individual medical evidence
The amount of cover an employer can provide without paying any premium
The maximum benefit any single member can receive
The excess a member pays before a claim is met
questions.explanation: Below the free cover limit, members are covered automatically; above it, the insurer may ask for medical evidence before accepting the extra. 'Free' refers to freedom from evidence, not from cost.

questions.stem: What is an employee assistance programme (EAP)?
options: A scheme that pays employees' NHS prescription charges
An employer's formal process for managing poor performance
A confidential service giving staff access to a helpline, short-term counselling and practical advice
An insurer's team that decides whether claims are paid
questions.explanation: An EAP is a wellbeing add-on covering emotional, money, legal and family worries in confidence. It sits alongside insurance cover rather than deciding claims.

questions.stem: A 200-person employer's PMI renewal arrives with a large price increase after a year of heavy musculoskeletal claims. What's the broker's most useful first response?
options: Accept the increase, because insurers' renewal rates can't be negotiated
Ask the employer for a list of which named employees made claims
Recommend cancelling the scheme straight away to avoid the cost
Analyse the claims data, challenge the insurer's assumptions, and look at options such as market testing or design changes
questions.explanation: The renewal is where brokers earn their keep: understanding what drove claims, pushing back, and finding fixes like an excess, a physio pathway or another insurer. Named people's health data is special category data and isn't needed for this.

questions.stem: A member of a client's PMI scheme has a claim declined because the insurer says the condition is chronic. The member disagrees and calls the broker. What should the broker do?
options: Review the policy wording and the medical facts, and take it up with the insurer on the member's behalf if the decision looks wrong
Tell the member the insurer's decision is final and can't be questioned
Pay the claim from the broker's own funds to keep the client happy
Advise the member to cancel and buy a moratorium policy elsewhere
questions.explanation: Claims support and advocacy are a core part of the service, because the broker acts for the client, not the insurer. If it still isn't resolved, the member can complain and, where eligible, take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

questions.stem: Poppy's friend has PMI through work and notices a new lump. What's usually the right first step to use the policy?
options: Go straight to a private hospital and send the bill to the insurer afterwards
See a GP, NHS or the insurer's virtual GP, for a referral, then contact the insurer to pre-authorise before booking
Go to A&E first so the visit is recorded for the claim
Wait until the scheme renews to check whether lumps are covered
questions.explanation: A GP referral is the usual gateway into private care, and pre-authorisation confirms cover before costs are run up. Booking without a referral or authorisation risks the claim not being paid.

questions.stem: Which statement about PMI and the NHS is true?
options: Taking out PMI means opting out of NHS care
PMI pays the NHS to treat its members faster
PMI complements the NHS: members still use it for emergencies, GP care and long-term conditions
PMI is designed to cover everything the NHS provides
questions.explanation: PMI mainly buys faster access, choice and comfort for planned acute treatment. Emergencies, everyday GP care and long-term conditions stay with the NHS, which members remain fully entitled to use.

questions.stem: Which statement about consultants in the UK is true?
options: Consultants must choose between the NHS and private practice and can never do both
Private hospitals only employ consultants who have left the NHS
PMI members are treated by GPs rather than consultants
Many consultants hold an NHS post and also see private patients
questions.explanation: It's common for a consultant to work in the NHS and run a private practice alongside it, so an insured patient may see the same specialist as an NHS one, just sooner.

questions.stem: What is generally seen as the main driver of demand for PMI in the UK?
options: Pressure on NHS waiting lists for diagnosis and planned treatment
A legal requirement for employers to provide health insurance
The NHS no longer treating acute conditions
PMI premiums becoming cheaper than NHS prescription charges
questions.explanation: When waits for scans and planned operations grow, people and employers look for faster access. There's no legal duty on employers to offer PMI; it's a voluntary benefit.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how a clinical background helps in health broking?
options: It means the broker can diagnose members and decide their treatment
It helps you understand pathways and conditions, see what a claim means for a person, and talk to clinicians and HR on equal terms
It removes the need to learn insurance law and regulation
It is mainly useful for calculating the premium rates insurers charge
questions.explanation: Clinical knowledge sharpens benefit design, claims conversations and credibility, but brokers don't give clinical advice, and insurance and regulatory knowledge is still essential.
